66.t: Lester Young replaces Ben Webster; the era of well-trained musicians
66.s: Lester Young joined Kirk after Webster left for Cab Calloway, before going to Basie. She compares Lester's freedom with Webster's economy, and says the era bred Parker and Dizzy.
66.ch: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
66.q: When Ben Webster left (the) Andy Kirk to join Cab Calloway, Lester Young joined us in Kansas City, but he didn't stay with us very long because shortly after that he went to Count Basie's band.

378.t: Trumbauer's influence on Lester Young and Benny Carter
378.s: Benny Carter and Lester Young both told him Trumbauer was an idol, Lester copying his C-melody sound, and Norvo says to compare the records.
378.q: -- in fact he died in Kansas City and -- and his wife still lives there in Kansas City. And he said that he used to try to imitate the sound of the C-melody saxophone, the sound that Frankie Trumbauer got on tenor.

28.t: Lester Young and his intentional shock
28.s: Butler first heard Lester on clarinet in Moten's band, discusses Herschel Evans, Chu Berry and Don Byas, and sees Lester as an intentional shocker and individualist younger than Hawkins.
28.ch: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
28.q: Well, Lester Young struck me as a -- first, I heard him play the clarinet. See, I heard him play in Moten's band the clarinet and I heard him -- Herschel Evans play the tenor saxophone. And Herschel Evans, see, Herschel Evans had lived what it seemed like, because Chu Berry had been around there…

380.t: Lester Young after the Army, and the union rule at the Capri
380.s: Callender describes Lester's depression, his drinking, and the six-month union wait that kept him to specialty spots at the Capri.
380.ch: Los Angeles, Ellington and the recording scene
380.q: Yeah. He would tell me some of the things... At that time, I guess he'd... Well, anybody who smoked pot was considered a dope fiend. So he was considered a dope fiend! And naturally he resented that, because he wasn't! He was an ordinary person like the rest of us. I mean, who didn't smoke pot? I…

382.t: The Apollo program and Campbell's record collection
382.s: They recall a program about the Apollo Theater and Campbell's priceless albums.
382.q: I heard on this Benny Carter album, I played it today and there's a selection on that, I didn't get time to look at it because I was busy doing something else, but there's a passage in fact it sounds just like "One O'Clock Jump" the beginning of "One O'Clock Jump." I forget the title of the tune.…

758.s: Roy says Lester sounded when they first met as he did later.
758.q: : Well, I think... You say the same way. All I know, he was a good player. I liked the way he played. I couldn't say the same way or...

232.t: The Douglas Brothers, Paul Quinichette and Elon Watkins
232.s: Kansas City's Douglas brothers epitomized the local style but stayed home, as did Elon Watkins after Hampton raided Fields' band.
232.q: Yes. Elon didn't stay with Hamp and I inquired later and Hamp said he was all right, he just came on back to Tulsa, you know, some of them just don't go for it.

18.s: Young was quiet and only played his horn; they made records and gigs together.
18.q: : He was O.K. We made some recordings together and we played gigs together. He was quiet; he didn't do nothing but play his horn.

93.t: Lester Young plays Let the Good Times Roll for his warm-up
93.s: While Green warmed up on stage, young Lester Young played along with Let the Good Times Roll, later Symphony Sid's theme.
93.q: Yes. They even started to imitate them. The improvisations that the tap dancers did, in their tap dancing. --like say, for instance, They began to realize that it was jazz (Unintelligible) Lester Young -- the late, great Lester Young. He composed a piece called "Let the Good Times Roll" and I was…

235.s: He never met Herschel Evans but admired him, and chose Herschel's heavy tone over Lester's light one.
235.ch: First jobs and finding his sound
235.q: No. No, I never met him, he died very young. Yeah. He was a Coleman Hawkins disciple and, from what I understand, everybody just loved him, you know what I mean, because he had a certain style about him, not only playing, but as a person. Certain characteristics that everybody admired and obviously…

388.t: Babe Russin and shared Basie-Ellington tastes
388.s: Tenor saxophonist Babe Russin was the first in the band to mention Lester Young and shared Leeman's love of Basie and Ellington over Dorsey's style.
388.q: And he's still writing. And we had Babe Russin in that band, he's a great tenor saxophone player, and he was one of the first people that accepted Prez.

115.t: A digression: Leonard Chadwick, the Blue Devils and a photograph
115.s: Looking at a picture, Gus recalls Chadwick and the Blue Devils, Ernest Williams, Doc Ross and Lester Young.
115.ch: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
115.q: He used to sing, he was the singer in the band. Let's see, who else -- Doc Ross, Lester Young.

237.s: Lovett only talked with Lester Young in Kansas City, and Goodwin knew him as a very young, learning player.
237.ch: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
237.q: I knew him here in Kansas City, yes, but that was the first time I ever met him, here in Kansas City.

75.t: Playing with Lester Young in New York and Canada
75.s: He toured Canada with Lester Young's group with Lee Young, Bumps Myers and bassist Jesus, and again with Kirby.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: Toronto, yes, I played with him there. We toured Canada. The second time I toured Canada was with John Kirby. See, John Kirby would be near the end of that era, because the war was coming to a close. So it would be in '45... That's the time when "Lover Man" started coming out.

7.t: Meeting Lester Young and his family in Minneapolis
7.s: Thomas recalls dance work around the Twin Cities and meeting Prez, his father and brother Lee, then seeing Lester with King Oliver in Kansas City and finding him scared of New York.
7.q: So Minneapolis... I stayed with a good family in Minneapolis. And I played in this little band. We played all over town. We played all the big dances. Because one of the dance halls was right on my side of the town where we lived. And then we played for dances in St. Paul.

455.t: Keg goes to Minneapolis; Lester Young arrives with the Blue Devils
455.s: Keg writes about a sax player named Lester Young; the Blue Devils come to Kansas City with Lester, whom Budd compares to Trumbauer.
455.ch: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
455.q: Well, during that time, along then in the town was Walter Paige and his Blue Devils, and when he came in town he had this sax@phone player which my brother had been writing to me. My brother and I had separated by this time.

529.t: Stylists versus players: Hawkins, Young, Miles and Dizzy
529.s: Sam separates stylists like Lester Young and Miles from fine players like Chu Berry and Dizzy.
529.q: Yeah because they have a different style of playing and what he does, he does well, you know. He have a following in each of their field. Like Lester Young, he had a following. Coleman Hawkins had a following and they both was fantastic saxophone players. They both were stylists.

13.t: Meeting Lester Young when he sat in for Cecil Irwin
13.s: Young filled in at the Orpheum in Minneapolis.
13.q: I think we just filled out that engagement at the theater there. It was a split week. And I don't know whether it was the Friday, Saturday, Sunday, or whether it was Thursday. It was a split week. I know he finished out the engagement. Three days or four days. Then I think we came home after that.
